name: Blood Oxygen (SpO₂)
steps: Warm your hand and remove any nail polish.
Clip the oximeter on a fingertip and keep the hand still at heart level.
Wait until the number is steady and record it.
when: Daily. Twice a day while Yellow; recheck in 5 minutes and check cabin O₂/CO₂.
mistakes: Cold fingers, which give a falsely low number.
Nail polish or a loose clip.
Moving the hand during the reading.
Writing down the first number before it settles.
escalate_if: Shortness of breath, confusion or blue lips.
why: SpO₂ shows how well the lungs move oxygen into the blood. A drop can come from a cabin leak, low oxygen, a rising CO₂ level or a lung problem.
benefits: Backs up the cabin CO₂ reading on the same node.

yellow: Warm your hand and recheck in 5 minutes.
Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ displays.
Measure twice a day until Green.
red: Check cabin O₂/CO₂ and turn on fans.
If it is below 90%, give supplemental oxygen per the crew medical checklist.

name: Cabin CO₂ Pressure (ppCO₂)
steps: Open the cabin air panel. The sensor reports automatically.
Read the current ppCO₂ and the 7-day average.
If it is rising, check fans and the CO₂ scrubber.
mistakes: Reading only the average and missing local pockets of CO₂ around your face.
Ignoring headaches that appear before the alarm.
Sleeping or working in a dead-air spot with no airflow.
escalate_if: Headache, tiredness, blurred vision or nausea.
why: In weightlessness, exhaled CO₂ does not rise away from your face. CO₂ also widens blood vessels in the brain, which adds to pressure behind the eyes. Astronauts feel symptoms at much lower CO₂ than people on Earth.
benefits: Helps explain headaches and high ONSD.
Shows if the scrubber needs attention.

red: Do all the Yellow steps now.
Inspect the CO₂ removal system (CDRA) and sorbent beds.
Tell the Crew Medical Officer and ground (if reachable).

name: Fasting Blood Glucose

baseline.text: 90 ± 8 mg/dL (typical 75–105; insulin resistance is common in space)

steps: Measure in the morning after at least 8 hours without food. Wash and dry your hands.
Prick the side of a fingertip and touch the drop to the test strip.
Wait for the result and record the number.
when: Weekly in the morning, fasting. Daily while Yellow or Red; recheck in 15 minutes if low (under 70).
mistakes: Measuring after eating or drinking anything but water.
Treating a low and a high result the same way.
escalate_if: Confusion, shaking or sweating, which can mean low glucose.
why: Without gravity and normal exercise load, the body can become less sensitive to insulin. A creeping rise shows early. A low reading is an emergency of its own, which is why the steps for high and low are different.
benefits: Avoids treating low glucose the wrong way.
Gives the flight surgeon a 7-day trend.

yellow: Measure daily until it returns to Green.
Keep up ARED and aerobic exercise.
red_high: Repeat the fasting test tomorrow morning.
Keep up ARED and aerobic exercise.
Send the 7-day trend to the flight surgeon.
red_low: Take 15 g of fast carbohydrate now (glucose tablets or fruit juice).
Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat the carbohydrate if still under 70.
If you are confused or unresponsive, a crewmate starts emergency care and gives nothing by mouth.

name: Skin Status

yellow.text: 1–2: small mild rash, contact dermatitis or lunar-dust irritation

red.text: 3: spreading, blistering or painful rash (such as shingles), or any rash with fever

steps: Look over your skin, especially hands, arms, neck and any area touched by suit or dust.
Take a clear photo of any rash or change, in good light, with a size reference.
Pick the category (0–3) that fits best and record it.
when: Weekly. Take a photo daily while Yellow or Red.
mistakes: Photos in poor light or out of focus.
Ignoring a small rash that is spreading.
Forgetting to check temperature when there is a rash.
escalate_if: Any rash together with a fever.
A painful, one-sided or blistering rash.
why: Closed habitats have floating dust and mould, and lunar or Mars dust irritates skin. A weaker immune system in space can also wake up dormant viruses that show up as a rash, such as shingles.
benefits: Photos let the flight surgeon help from a distance.
Links to the WBC and temperature checks.

yellow: Vacuum the habitat with the HEPA filter.
red: Take clear photos and send them to the flight surgeon at once (store-and-forward).
Do not start any treatment until authorized per the crew medical checklist.
